A1.justification: Both PDFs describe YouTube-Occ, and their text, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial revision. All pages were inspected, including v1's concluding NeurIPS checklist. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate scientific appendix.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original pre-training, limited-annotation, cross-dataset and zero-shot experimental results for the proposed approach.

after.justification: Section 5 reports original pseudo-label evaluations, experiments across multiple architectures, data-scaling comparisons and component ablations.

M1.justification: v1 back-projects pixels into voxels and contrasts pooled superpixel/supervoxel features. v2 replaces this correspondence mechanism with voxel-anchored Gaussian rendering into the image plane and adds an online class-prototype memory bank and cross-scene contrastive loss. These substantially change the pre-training procedure and objective.

E1.justification: Both versions use NYUv2, Occ-ScanNet and YouTube-Occ for indoor semantic occupancy prediction. The larger Internet-video collection, additional architectures and revised label fractions change experimental settings without establishing a new domain, population or task.

E2.justification: The NYUv2 comparison adds ISO and EmbodiedOcc; the Occ-ScanNet comparison adds EmbodiedOcc++ and RoboOcc. v2 Table 4 additionally evaluates HASSC, GaussRender and Pri3D against the proposed training strategy, substantially broadening v1's architecture and random-initialization comparisons.

E3.justification: YouTube-Occ grows from 14,592 to 100,372 frames, with a new 50K-subset comparison. Pre-training is evaluated on three architectures instead of only Symphonies. The stated pre-training learning rate changes from 8e-4 to 2e-4, and Occ-ScanNet/YouTube-Occ training changes from 30 to 10 epochs. v2 also adds pseudo-label and joint-training controls and revises the evaluated label fractions.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's annotation-efficiency and qualitative analyses, v2 adds pseudo-label quality and naive-supervision diagnostics, a 50K-versus-full-data scaling analysis, and component ablations. Tables 5–6 isolate the two losses and test projection choices, learnable Gaussian parameters, prototype momentum and semantic thresholding.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, uncertainty estimates or significance tests. v1 explicitly acknowledges 'No error bars' in its checklist; that acknowledgment disappears, but v2 retains the same point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: The main proposed-method NYUv2 result changes from 30.74/51.12 to 31.65/52.15 mIoU/IoU. Occ-ScanNet changes from 58.15/67.75 to 49.38/61.25, while its Symphonies baseline also changes from 57.85/67.50 to 47.71/59.89. Numerous architecture, scaling, strategy and ablation results are added, and the NYUv2 zero-shot result is removed. These are revised results under changed methods/settings, not controlled cross-version performance gains or losses.

T1.justification: v2 adds mathematical definitions for class prototypes, the prototype contrastive loss and the combined objective in Equations 3–4. The region loss retains the earlier contrastive form. This is a limited extension of the formal objectives; no theorem, proof or theoretical guarantee is introduced.

C1.justification: v1's abstract claims state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on both benchmarks; v2 instead emphasizes consistent pre-training gains across architectures, especially with limited labels. The methodological contribution is redefined around Gaussian rendering and prototype alignment, and the failure of naive pseudo-label supervision becomes a central claim. The Internet-video occupancy novelty claim remains.

C2.justification: v2 introduces geometric-scale and semantic-taxonomy mismatch as conjectured explanations for weak pseudo-label supervision, and interprets the new alignment mechanisms as addressing noisy supervision. Its limitations now include invisible/occluded voxels, extension to temporal or multi-view networks, and dependence on the wall-height assumption. v1 mainly emphasized object-level grouping and identified dynamic/static separation as future work.

D1.justification: v2 adds class-name prompting instructions, Gaussian parameterization details and the default prototype momentum of 0.999. It promises public code and data, whereas v1 withheld the dataset and promised code upon acceptance; actual release is not established. Conversely, v1's explicit YouTube train/validation counts and Occ-ScanNet scene-disjoint resplitting description are omitted.

R1.justification: New Section 4.3 explicitly distinguishes the approach from GaussTR, AGO, AutoOcc and other outdoor self-supervised methods through calibration assumptions and architectural coupling. References and discussion also expand to alternative training strategies and the manual occupancy-annotation pipeline, while v1's CrossPoint/MM-Point discussion disappears. This materially revises research positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. The narrative now develops manual annotation, automated curation and pseudo-label failure before presenting the revised framework; experiments are reorganized around pipeline evaluation, pre-training and ablations. The checklist is removed, and authorship, affiliations and acknowledgments are updated.

P2.justification: The document adopts a different layout and substantially restructures its displays. Figures 1–2 are retained with resizing/relocation, and v1 Figure 4 becomes v2 Figure 5. The NYUv2 qualitative figure and radar plots disappear; new framework and pseudo-label figures appear. Benchmark and few-shot displays are consolidated, with new strategy and ablation tables.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important evidentiary weaknesses: multiple-architecture tests support model-agnostic applicability, Table 4 adds relevant competing training strategies, and Tables 5–6 test component contributions absent from v1. It also replaces the unsupported abstract claim of state-of-the-art zero-shot performance with claims centered on demonstrated pre-training benefits and states more specific limitations. Statistical uncertainty remains unreported, and omitted split documentation weakens reproducibility, but the new comparisons and diagnostic evidence substantially strengthen the paper overall.
